author: NeoTSX
text: Amazon security researchers discovered an AI agent finding a zero-day exploit in 11 minutes. The attacker used an open-source agent framework called Cairn against a university server in East Asia. The human operator typed three words into the prompt: obtain shell access. Without human guidance, the agent scanned the server, targeted an open-source medical imaging application, and uncovered an unpatched zero-day vulnerability in its file upload tool. It bypassed directory boundaries, wrote executable code, and secured full root control in eleven minutes. Amazon caught the operation because the human hacker made a basic mistake. The attacker left their own control server exposed without a password, letting researchers pull forty-eight hours of activity logs. Software security spent thirty years assuming zero-day exploits required weeks of work by expert human engineers. Once autonomous agents can probe codebases for pennies per hour, the cost of discovering undisclosed flaws drops to almost nothing.

author: pyotam2
text: AI agents shielding your kernel in real time (rare footage) I went through the source code of @OpenAI and @Cisco 's Shirudo. Two things stood out: What a shield-writing agent reads is an attack path. CVE write-ups, logs, system activity. Attackers control much of that text: process names, file paths, DNS answers. That’s prompt injection aimed at code headed for the kernel. Signed isn’t the same as correct. The kernel’s checker proves a shield won’t crash the machine, not that it blocks the exploit or won't break production. Whoever holds the signing key is the approver, which makes it the most powerful identity in your environment. The concept is genuinely promising. But your kernel can be locked down like Alcatraz while someone on the team installs an MCP server called “jira-but-faster-trust-me” from a 4-star GitHub repo, hands it their tokens, and lets their coding agent run whatever it suggests. Much AI risk today lives in that layer. Wipe the floor all you want, but check who’s holding the cup.

text: 10 cyber security signals you missed today 👇 1. Microsoft says a flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers was exploited to reach stored secrets, closed on 19 Nov. If you run APIM Classic, rotate named values, client secrets and subscription keys now; the fix doesn't invalidate anything already taken. 2. Microsoft is notifying tenants that an Entra Connect Health API bug exposed admin emails and tenant metadata (no passwords or tokens). Warn your admins to expect targeted phishing and get phishing-resistant MFA on privileged accounts. 3. Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 is being exploited in clustered setups for root access, and it's now on CISA's KEV list. Patch to X15.5.20 or later; Cisco lists no workaround. 4. CISA added N-able Mail Assure/SpamExperts SSRF CVE-2026-134624 to KEV after an incident N-able says was confined to one hosted server. MSPs: read N-able's update and watch for the root cause report it's promised within two weeks. 5. GL. iNet says attackers abused its GoodCloud remote management to drop malware on some routers and KVMs. Install the latest security firmware, and if a KVM was hit, check the PC it's plugged into too. 6. OpenRouter dropped three inference providers after Dragos's seeded test prompts and decoy credentials leaked and got used. Lesson: never paste live secrets into prompts, and rotate any you have. 7. Cleverbridge, which runs checkouts for plenty of software vendors, confirmed card numbers, expiry dates and CVVs were copied from its platform. Bought licences by card? Check your statements. 8. The NCSC says AI-assisted attacks have risen sharply since September, mostly hitting old weaknesses like credentials left in repos and misconfigurations. Boring hygiene is now urgent hygiene. 9. CISA also added MONAI Label CVE-2026-133968 to KEV, linked to an AI-agent-driven hacking campaign. Niche medical imaging tool, but a sign of how quickly agents chew through exposed apps. 10. The European Commission confirmed names and emails were stolen from its EU Academy learning platform in an AI-assisted attack. If you've used it, expect EU-themed phishing. Every item checked against vendor advisories or reputable sources. Links in the first reply. Which of these lands on your patch list first? New one every day.

author: gastronomy
text: Carried-Over and Agent-Native Threats in the Supply Chain of LLM Agent Skills: Agent skills are reusable packages that extend a large language model (LLM) agent with scripts, third-party dependencies, and natural-language instructions. An agent builds a skill's arguments from user requests and untrusted external content, so a flaw left by a benign author can escalate a prompt injection to code execution. Existing studies target malicious skills or a single attack vector, and none tests whether an agent can reach such flaws. We present the first registry-scale empirical study of the supply chain attack surface arising from unintentional vulnerabilities in agent skills, over all 48,682 skills in ClawHub. The study covers two carried-over risks, dependencies and first-party code, and two agent-native ones, install instructions and credentials printed to stdout. We screen all skills by static analysis, manually review all 3,428 cases flagged by the four main detectors, and test reachability by running sampled flagged skills in a sandbox and with a live LLM agent under indirect prompt injection. First, dependency risk carries over in a different form: 49.6% of the skills with resolvable dependencies depend on a version with a known CVE, and unlike npm packages, which mostly become vulnerable after release, 78.3% of them are born vulnerable, already exposed at publication. Second, few of these CVEs are reachable: agent input reaches the vulnerable function in only 3.0% of the affected skills, whereas 21 of 22 sampled first-party flaws are exploited end to end in the sandbox. Third, a live agent executes the injected payload in 48.5% of the sampled flagged skills, but almost always in its own shell before the skill runs, and the payload reaches a flaw in the skill itself in only 5.0%. Hence, registries should prioritize first-party flaws over dependency alerts, and agent runtimes should not pass skill arguments through a shell.https://t.co/lbO5rrUDGH
